chapter: Advice to youth and the art of drumming
title: Showmanship versus musicianship and fewer drum solos
summary: He says Twenties bands had to be hot visually, but audiences now want arrangements and rarely hear long drum solos.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: That sort of thing really has hurt the art of drumming and it's hurt drummers being --

Well, it would have been all right if they had elected -- see, in the era they were coming up, this was the Roaring Twenties and all of that type of thing and all that, and there were so many things that were accepted then, and expected then. Like, a black band was the hot band. They had to play the hot music, and maybe they'd have another band over here playing the sweet things and the soft things, and then a hot band. And so, to get hot they had to do a little bit of everything -- visual and playing.
That carries over. I know a lot of people go to hear a combo or a big band, and they go there to watch the drummer.
They don't go there to watch --

Oh, no, but, see, that's showmanship. But, really, today the people are more musical conscious. They like to hear these beautiful arrangements, they like to hear these beautiful -- I mean, the exact sounds and great soloists and all of this type of a thing. And it has taken away from that period. You don't need that now, no.
So now -- and this is the thing, when you're

listening to a band, I mean, you hear the big band in concert, you don't hardly hear drum solos hardly, too much, even here. I mean, extended drum solos. You may hear eight bars or something like that, or 16, but that's about it. You don't hear a lot of drum solos, that much.
